body.p: Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 47, and 135-145, 147, and 148 were previously pending in this application.1 By this amendment, claims 1, 30, 37, 42, 47, 135-139, and 142 have been amended and are supported by the specification as originally filed, for example, on page 13, lines 17-19; page 14, lines 20-30; page 19, lines 8-9 and 16-22; and page 25, lines 21-26. No new matter has been added.
Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 47, 135-145, 147, and 148 are currently pending in this application for examination, with claim 1 being independent.
Representatives Tani Chen, Reg. No. 52,728, and Steven F. Hannigan, Reg. No. 80,498,

("the Representatives") thank Examiner Thompson for the courtesy of a videoconference interview conducted on August 12, 2022. During the interview, the rejection of independent claim 1 and associated dependent claims under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over U.S. Pat. Apl. Pub. No. 2013/0338627 to Rylander et al. ("Rylander") in view of U.S. Pat. Apl. Pub. No. 2005/0161594 to Hollingsworth et al. ("Hollingsworth"), in view of U.S. Pat. Apl. Pub. No. 2011/0208031 to Wolfe et al. ("Wolfe"), and further in view of U.S. Pat. Apl. Pub. No. 2011/0207237 to Sai et al. ("Sai") was discussed. The Representatives discussed with Examiner Thompson three proposed amendments to independent claim 1 and further indicated that there would no motivation for a person of ordinary skill in the art to combine Rylander and Wolfe. Examiner Thompson noted that the function and/or intended use of a device does not patentably distinguish the device over the prior art, referring to MPEP §§ 2114 and 2111.04. Examiner Thompson further suggested that the claims be amended to define structural distinctions that differentiate the claims over the cited references. Further responsive remarks to each of the bases of rejection are now presented.

The Patent Office states that the recitation "at least one particle attached to the end portion of the member and configured to facilitate analysis of the cell" in independent claim 1 is unclear. Without acceding to the correctness of the rejection, independent claim 1 has been amended to recite that at least one particle attached to the end portion of the member is configured to facilitate analysis of the cell by interacting with an analyte from the cell such that a characteristic of the analyte is determined by light propagated through the member. Withdrawal of the claim rejections of this ground is respectfully requested.

The Patent Office also states that claims 30, 37, and 135-139 are unclear because there is insufficient antecedent basis for "the particle." See pages 3-4 of the Office Action. As suggested by the Patent Office, claims 30, 37, and 135-139 have been amended to recite "the at least one particle." Withdrawal of the claim rejections on this ground is respectfully requested.

The Patent Office also states that claim 42 is unclear because there is insufficient antecedent basis for "particles." See page 4 of the Office Action. Claim 42 has been amended to recite "wherein the end portion of the member is coated with a plurality of particles." Withdrawal of the claim rejections on this ground is respectfully requested.

h1.u: 103 in view of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai

body.p: U.S.C. § 103(a) as allegedly being unpatentable over Rylander in view of Hollingsworth, in view of Wolfe, and further in view of Sai.

The Patent Office alleges that Rylander teaches each and every feature of independent claim 1, except for: (i) the end portion having a diameter of less than 100 nm, which the Patent Office alleges is taught by Hollingsworth; (ii) at least one particle attached to the end portion of the member, which the Patent Office alleges is taught by Wolfe; and (iii) the at least one particle attached to the end portion of the member is configured to facilitate analysis of the cell, which the Patent Office alleges is taught by Sai (see pages 5-9 of the Office Action).
L Rylander fails to teach or suggest a member comprising an end portion that is configured for insertion into a cell while maintaining viability of the cell

Without acceding to the merits of the rejection, independent claim 1 has been amended to recite that the end portion of the member is configured for insertion into the cell while maintaining viability of the cell. Rylander fails to teach or suggest at least this feature. Instead, Rylander discloses systems for delivering exogenous photoabsorbers such as nanoparticles (e.g., single-wall carbon nanohorns or SWNHs) to tissue regions for targeted cancer treatment (e.g., destruction) of cancer cells. See, for example, paragraphs [0295]-[0300] of Rylander. In particular, paragraph [0299] of Rylander states, "The present invention discloses the ability to add targeting molecules to the SWNHs and shown selective photothermal destruction of tumor cells." In addition, paragraph [0300] of Rylander states, "The present invention discloses the ability to destroy tumor cells when laser irradiation at 1064 nm was used in combination with SWNHs."

Indeed, it is not surprising that Rylander fails to teach or suggest a member comprising an end portion configured for insertion into a cell and having a substantially constant average cross- sectional diameter of less than 100 nm, as conceded by the Patent Office, since Rylander is not concerned with maintaining cell viability, but instead is directed to systems configured to perform cancer therapy by inducing photothermal or photochemical damage to target tissue. As evidenced by Makvandi, P., et al., Nano-Micro Lett., 2021, 13, 93 ("Makvandi"), submitted herewith, microneedles, such as those described in Rylander, must be configured to pierce the human stratum corneum (-10 to 20 micrometers) without rupturing or bending during penetration. See, for example, the Abstract of Makvandi. The flat microneedles in Rylander, for example, have a tip diameter ranging from 9-139 micrometers, while the sharp microneedles in Rylander have a tip diameter ranging from 2-8 micrometers, as shown in Tables 3 and 4, respectively. The smallest tip diameter disclosed in Rylander (i.e., 2 micrometers) is therefore more than an order of magnitude larger than the average cross-sectional diameter of the end portion of the member as recited in independent claim 1.
Page 25, lines 9-26 of the specification as originally filed in conjunction with FIG. 4E describes that a fiber tip probe (FTP) having a tip diameter in the micrometer range (e.g., 5

micrometers) causes cell death after puncturing the cell, while a FTP having a tip diameter less than 100 nm maintains cell viability. In addition, as evidenced by Kim, W., et al., J. Am. Chem. Soc., 2007, 129, 7228-7229 ("Kim"), submitted herewith, the viability of cells shows strong dependence on the size of nanowires used to pierce the cells. When large diameter (-400 nm) nanowires were used, cell death occurred within a day, whereas small diameter (-30 nm) nanowires preserved cell life for more than 5 days. See, for example, the paragraph bridging pages 7228 and 7229 of Kim. Furthermore, Ryu, S., et al., J. Biosci. Bioeng., 2013, 116, 3, 391-396 ("Ryu"), also submitted herewith, states that insertion of a nanoneedle 200 nm in diameter has no significant effect on cell viability even after 1 hour of insertion. See, for example, page 394, first full paragraph of Ryu. In view of the instant specification, Kim, and Ryu, a person of ordinary skill in the art would have recognized that the microneedles described in Rylander, having a tip diameter of at least 2 micrometers, would induce cell death upon cell penetration.
II. There would have been no motivation for a person of ordinary skill in the art to combine Rylander and Wolfe in the manner suggested by the Patent Office

The Patent Office states that Rylander fails to teach at least one particle attached to the end portion of the member, wherein (i) the at least one particle is positioned in an optically interrogatable position with respect to light transmitted through the member to the end portion, (ii) the at least one particle is attached to end portion of the member via an adhesive positioned between the at least one particle and the end portion of the member, and (iii) the adhesive comprises at least one of a polymer or an epoxy. The Patent Office alleges that Wolfe cures the deficiencies of Rylander and that it would have been obvious for a person of ordinary skill in the art to modify the end portion of the member of Rylander to further comprise at least one particle attached to the end portion of the member by an adhesive, because Wolfe teaches that at least one particle attached to the end portion of the member by an adhesive employs surface enhancement to boost signal detection of the neural probe when molecules of interest are in close proximity. See pages 7-9 of the Office Action.
Rylander is generally directed to microneedles for light-based therapeutics that are inserted into the skin. See, for example, the Abstract and paragraph [0162] of Rylander. As discussed

above, the microneedles in Rylander are configured to deliver exogenous photoabsorbers (e.g., nanoparticles) to specific tissue regions for targeted treatment (e.g., cancer treatment). See, for example, paragraphs [0295]-[0300] of Rylander. In particular, paragraph [0297] of Rylander states, "... devices and methods of the present invention may be sized appropriately to interface with existing clinical cystoscopes permitting optical image guidance to deliver nanoparticles to the tumor site." Upon delivery to the target site, the nanostructures absorb infrared irradiation for enhanced tumor destruction. See, for example, paragraph [0299] of Rylander.

Wolfe is generally directed to a neural probe that includes a metallic trace provided along the length of the probe, and one or more contacts provided on the tip of the probe, wherein the metallic trace terminates at the one or more contacts. See, for example, the Abstract of Wolfe. The one or more contacts of the neural probe may include an array of nanostructures. See, for example, paragraph [0067]. The nanostructures function as a Raman scattering sensor that can obtain compositional information of local brain tissue. See, for example, paragraphs [0054] and [0073] of Wolfe.
A person of ordinary skill in the art would have recognized that if the exogenous

photoabsorbers in Rylander were attached to the microneedle via an adhesive, then the microneedle would be incapable of delivering the photoabsorbers to target tissue. Such a modification would render Rylander unsatisfactory for its intended purpose of performing cancer therapy by inducing photothermal or photochemical damage to target tissue via the photoabsorbers. See, for example, MPEP § 2143.01(V). Indeed, if the nanoparticles in Rylander were attached to the microneedle via an adhesive, as suggested by the combination of Rylander and Wolfe proposed by the Patent Office, then the microneedle in Rylander would not be able to perform photothermal therapeutics and cancer treatment.
HI. Summary

For at least the reasons outlined above, the combination of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai does not render amended independent claim 1 obvious, and claim 1 is believed to be patentable over the combination of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai. The remaining claims that stand rejected on this ground depend from independent claim 1, and are therefore also

patentable over the combination of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai for at least the reasons outlined above. In addition, it is not conceded that Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, or Sai, alone or in combination, teach or render obvious any of the features recited in claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 47, 135-138, 140-144, 147, and 148, as asserted by the Patent Office. It is also not conceded that it would have been obvious to combine Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai in the manner suggested by the Patent Office. Withdrawal of the claim rejections of this ground is respectfully requested.

h1.u: 103 in view of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, Sai, and Jun

body.p: Dependent claim 139 stands rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Rylander in view of Hollingsworth, in view of Sai, in view of Wolfe, and further in view of U.S. Pat. Apl. Pub. No. 2015/0092191 to Jung et al. ("Jung").
Claim 139 depends from independent claim 1, which is patentable over Rylander,

Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai for at least the reasons outlined above. Jung fails to cure the deficiencies of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai noted above with respect to independent claim 1. Accordingly, claim 139 is also patentable over the combination of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, Sai, and Jung. In addition, it is not conceded that Jung teaches any of the features recited in claim 139, and is it not conceded that it would have been obvious to combine Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, Sai, and Jung in the manner suggested in the Office Action. Withdrawal of the claim rejection on this ground is respectfully requested.
